items.item: Definition of Foundation Model: one model for many tasks vs traditional one-model-per-task
items.notes: Section 6.1 describes BERT/GPT/T5 as landmark models but does not crisply frame the FM paradigm (M1 face vs M2 car vs single FM). The slide's framing would strengthen the chapter opener.

items.item: Two FM types: representation models vs generative models
items.notes: Encoder/decoder distinction is covered architecturally but not labeled as representation vs generative FM categories.

items.item: Three adaptation methods diagram: Composition (frozen + head), Fine-Tuning, Prompting/ICL
items.notes: Fine-tuning and ICL are covered (Chapter 12, 16), but the unifying three-method taxonomy from Slide 3-6 (composition with adapter placement options: preprocessor, head, intermediate) is not presented as a single framework in chapter 6.

items.item: Image-side analogs: fine-tuning images, in-context/zero-shot classification by similarity to class prototypes
items.notes: Slides 4 and 7 show that the three adaptation strategies are modality-agnostic; Part II focuses on text. Could cite as a cross-reference to Part 5 (multimodal) but currently absent.

items.item: Encoder-only architecture reminder with fixed window 512 and [PAD] tokens
items.notes: Section 6.2 discusses MLM/CLM but does not explicitly recap encoder fixed-length window and [PAD] handling (slide 2). Minor gap, mostly covered in Part 1 tokenization.

items.item: Masked Language Modeling intuition: context vector must encode all surrounding context to enable token recovery
items.notes: Section 6.2.2 covers MLM clearly with the 15%/80/10/10 masking recipe and bidirectional context argument.

items.item: Next Sentence Prediction (NSP) and [CLS] token mechanics
items.notes: NSP and [CLS] are essentially absent from chapter 6/7 (only one stray '[CLS]' mention in 10.5 output). Slide 3, 5, 6, 7 describe [CLS] as sentence embedding via NSP loss; this foundational mechanism is not explained in the book.

items.item: [CLS] context vector reused as sentence embedding for downstream tasks; mean pooling as alternative
items.notes: Slide 6 explicitly explains the [CLS]-as-sentence-embedding pattern and mean-pooling alternative. Book does not mention this pooling strategy for sentence embeddings in chapter 6 or 7; embeddings come up later (chapter 31) but the chapter 6 link is missing.

items.item: Joint BERT loss: L = L_MLM + L_NSP
items.notes: Slide 7 shows the combined loss. Book covers MLM and CLM formulas but does not show the BERT joint objective.

items.item: RoBERTa: drops NSP, BPE tokenizer, single sentences and sentence pairs, outperforms BERT
items.notes: Section 6.1 'BERT Variants' covers RoBERTa improvements (more data, larger batches, drop NSP).

items.item: GPT decoder reminder: per-token context vector predicts next token via per-position classifier head
items.notes: Section 6.2.1 covers CLM clearly with the per-position prediction objective and the 'every token is a training signal' point.

items.item: Dataset preparation: shifted text pairs (tokens 1..n -> tokens 2..n+1)
items.notes: Code Fragment 6.2.1 explicitly implements label-shift for causal LM loss; matches slide 12 exactly.

items.item: Causal attention masking rationale and triangular mask implementation
items.notes: Section 6.2 figure 6.2.1 contrasts causal mask vs MLM; backbone covered in 3.1. Slide 13/14 (rationale + Python triangular mask) is well covered.

items.item: Python text generation inference loop using the trained decoder
items.notes: Section 6.9 lab includes generation code and section 4.1 covers autoregressive decoding.

items.item: Two motivations for explaining transformers: attention visualization for sanity check and feature importance for classification rationale
items.notes: Section 10.1 frames attention visualization and probing; section 10.3/10.4 cover feature attribution rationale.

items.item: Manually fetching attention matrices from HuggingFace with attention_mask and output_attentions
items.notes: Code Fragment 10.1.1 shows exactly this pattern (output_attentions=True, extract per-layer/per-head).

items.item: Printout of attention matrix with source token as query and per-head numerical patterns
items.notes: Heatmap plotting is covered (10.1.1); raw numerical printout per head (slide 5) is not shown, but it is a minor stylistic gap.

items.item: BertViz tool: interactive attention visualizer for BERT and GPT (encoded pair, all-heads, single-head, model view)
items.notes: Section 10.5.1.1 covers BertViz with head/model/neuron views; Code Fragment 10.5.10 and 10.4.3 include BertViz examples.

items.item: Naive single-token masking fails: 'not bad' worked example showing interaction invisibility
items.notes: Slide 12 has a memorable 'not bad' walkthrough showing why single-token masking misses interactions and motivates SHAP. Book covers SHAP but lacks this specific pedagogical example.

items.item: SHAP definition via game-theoretic Shapley values; average effect over all subsets; sampling approximation
items.notes: Section 10.3.1.2 covers SHAP for language models including the cooperative-game-theory framing and the cost of exact computation.

items.item: SHAP waterfall plot for house-price prediction: base 2.215 -> f(x) 2.846 read bottom-up
items.notes: Slide 14's concrete waterfall plot from home-price tabular SHAP is a memorable bridge; book talks about SHAP for LMs but does not show the canonical tabular waterfall illustration.

items.item: SHAP beeswarm plot across dataset: X = SHAP value, color = normalized feature value
items.notes: Slide 15's beeswarm view of dataset-level SHAP is not in the book; would strengthen 10.3.

items.item: Bar plot of mean absolute SHAP for overall feature importance in classification
items.notes: Section 10.3 discusses SHAP attributions but does not show the |mean SHAP| ranking plot pattern (slide 16).

items.item: Sentiment sentence colored red/blue by SHAP push toward positive/negative
items.notes: Section 10.3.5 (SHAP code) references shap.plots.text but the canonical color-coded sentence visualization from slide 17 is not embedded as a figure.

items.item: Why plain gradients underestimate importance: gradient saturation in trained models
items.notes: Section 10.3.1.1 explains IG and the gradient-saturation motivation.

items.item: Integrated Gradients: sum of gradients along baseline -> input path; interpretation 'features that help build up output'
items.notes: Section 10.3.1.1 has both the IG formula and the conceptual interpretation; Code Fragment 10.3.1 implements it from scratch.

items.item: transformer-interpret library: IG for HuggingFace transformers for sequence classification and target-class attribution
items.notes: Book promotes Captum (Code Fragment 10.3.3) but does not mention the transformer-interpret wrapper specifically. Adding it as a 'minimal HF API' alternative would help practitioners.

items.item: Captum is the PyTorch attribution library used for IG
items.notes: Section 10.5.1.1 'Captum: Meta's Attribution Toolkit' covers this fully with Code Fragment 10.5.2.

items.item: Captum applied to image classification with IG attributions
items.notes: Section 10.5 mentions Captum's breadth but does not show an image-classification IG example like slide 24.

items.item: Catalog figure of Captum's full attribution algorithm zoo
items.notes: Section 10.5 lists several Captum methods (Layer IG, GradientSHAP, Layer Conductance) but no compact 'algorithm zoo' figure like slide 25.

items.item: Original XLM model (Lample and Conneau 2019) as a multilingual encoder distinct from XLM-R
items.notes: Section 7.4 mentions only XLM-R (Conneau 2020). The earlier XLM with the explicit MLM + CLM + TLM training recipe (which slides 2-3 describe in detail) is not covered.

items.item: Three XLM losses: MLM (single-sentence), CLM (single-sentence next-token), TLM (Translation Language Modeling, mask token in one language recovered using the other)
items.notes: Slide 2-3 describe TLM as the key cross-lingual signal. Book does not introduce TLM as a pretraining objective in 6.2 or 7.4.

items.item: MLM vs TLM contrast figure: same-sentence recovery vs cross-lingual recovery
items.notes: Slide 3 has a clean side-by-side. Section 7.4 talks about cross-lingual transfer at the representation level but not the explicit pretraining objective comparison.

items.item: Cross-language tokenizer that uses word boundaries to share vocabulary across languages
items.notes: Section 7.4 discusses tokenization tax and vocabulary extension; the original XLM tokenizer split rule (slide 4) is a more granular implementation detail and is not explained.

items.item: Noam learning-rate schedule (Vaswani et al.): linear warmup then inverse-square-root decay
items.notes: Section 6.5.5 covers warmup, cosine decay, and WSD schedules but does not mention the original Noam schedule from 'Attention Is All You Need', which slide 6 highlights. This is a historical/pedagogical gap.

items.item: Noam scheduler PyTorch implementation
items.notes: No code example for Noam scheduler in book. Slide 7 shows the canonical reference implementation.

items.item: Batch class bundling source, target, and masks for translation training
items.notes: The classic Annotated Transformer Batch class (slide 9) is a useful pedagogical pattern; section 6.9 lab covers tiny GPT but not seq2seq translation.

items.item: End-to-end multilingual training loop with Batch + Noam optimizer
items.notes: No multilingual/seq2seq lab in chapter 6 or 7. Slide 10 walks through a translation training loop; could be appendix-grade material.

items.item: Translation inference and concrete example outputs
items.notes: Slides 11-12 show end-to-end translation examples; section 7.4 is largely conceptual on multilingual issues with no translation-specific runnable example.

top_5_must_add: Add a 'Foundation Models' framing callout in section 6.1 that contrasts one-model-per-task with one FM serving many tasks, names the three adaptation strategies (composition with frozen FM + task head, fine-tuning, prompting/ICL), and points to where each is covered later (chapters 12, 16, 17).

Add coverage of BERT's Next Sentence Prediction objective, the [CLS] sentence-embedding pattern, the mean-pooling alternative, and the joint MLM + NSP loss in section 6.2 (currently essentially absent across chapter 6 and 7).

Add a 'multilingual pretraining objectives' subsection in section 7.4 that introduces the original XLM model and the three losses (MLM, CLM, TLM = Translation Language Modeling), with the MLM vs TLM contrast diagram (slide 1311-3); currently only XLM-R is mentioned.

Add the Noam learning-rate schedule (linear warmup + inverse-square-root decay) to section 6.5.5 alongside cosine and WSD, with a short PyTorch implementation; it is the historical reference schedule from 'Attention Is All You Need' and is currently missing.

Strengthen section 10.3 SHAP coverage with the 'not bad' single-token-masking failure walkthrough (slide 1310-12), a tabular waterfall plot example, and a beeswarm visualization; also add a one-paragraph mention of transformer-interpret as a minimal HF wrapper around Captum IG.
